evidence: Reproducible physical screening with paper-tabulated material inputs and explicitly hypothetical process constraints. No partial-gravity experiment, validated product improvement or economic premium.

sic_epoxy.title: Improved Wear-Resistant Performance of Epoxy Resin Composites Using Ceramic Particles
sic_epoxy.access_scope: Full 17-page primary PDF retrieved; targeted reading of sections 2.1 and 4.1 and Table 4. Table 4 labels its entries theoretical data for a Stokes settling calculation. Source bytes are not locally pinned; this product hashes the explicit numerical transcription.
sic_epoxy.experimental_context: Kemapoxy 150 JM; medium SiC below 25 micrometres and fine SiC below 90 nm, 3-18 wt%; mixing for 4 minutes at 500 rpm, heating at 90 C for 1 minute, hydraulic pressing for 8 hours, final specimens 2 mm thick. Section 4.1 reports room-temperature settling images, about 45-minute pot life and nearly complete settling by 35 minutes. These conditions do not establish the illustrative 10-mm/100-second bubble-removal process.

paper_tabulated_material_inputs.evidence: The paper's theoretical calculation inputs, not new measurements. Fluid and particle densities are tabulated; the viscosity's measurement temperature is not specified. The 25-micrometre quantity is particle diameter, so the model uses a 12.5-micrometre radius.

illustrative_casting_process.evidence: Hypothetical geometry, bubble population, surface tension, uniformity tolerance and independently fixed liquid-processing interval. The cited paper does not supply this recipe, bubble size, surface tension or 100-second immobilization time.

long_interval_sensitivity.evidence: Hypothetical 45-minute hold at the same constant viscosity. The duration resembles the reported pot life, but viscosity evolves during curing; this is not a simulation of the published cure cycle. Failure of the three tested gravity environments does not mean that every intermediate gravity fails.

illustrative_spin_cast_geometry.evidence: Hypothetical fixed-focus, fixed-aperture comparison, not a transcription of a particular telescope. The equilibrium relation is omega^2=g/(2f); identical geometry/material gives a rotation-load proxy proportional to omega^2.

assumptions: Dilute, isolated spherical particles and bubbles in a Newtonian quiescent liquid; constant viscosity, radii, densities and surface tension; gas density neglected.
Bubble surface immobilized for the Stokes calculation. A clean mobile interface can change rise speed; no surfactant, concentration, wall, yield-stress or non-Newtonian correction is fitted.
All screened bubbles begin at the specified depth at time zero. Arrival at an accessible surface does not establish film rupture or gas escape; late bubble formation can invalidate clearance.
Particle uniformity is screened only by a displacement tolerance, not a measured concentration or finished-product property.

The same-mobility Earth controls must be considered. When both motions scale with g times the integral of inverse viscosity, freely changing the liquid interval or viscosity can erase the apparent fixed-cycle advantage.

The 100-second interval must be independently required by chemistry, filling, thermal history or another process constraint before it can support a location advantage. Optimize terrestrial degassing, pressure, rheology, particle size and curing controls in any comparison.
Ideal microgravity is represented by exactly zero acceleration. Residual acceleration, surface-driven transport and active bubble-removal systems are omitted.

The rotating-liquid screen assumes uniform axial gravity, a free surface in equilibrium and negligible capillary/edge effects. A solid export optic would additionally require controlled solidification, finishing and metrology; rotating orbital factories remain competitors.
